import json, os, sys
W = sys.argv[1]
def load(i): return json.load(open(os.path.join(W, 'drafts', i + '.json')))
def save(i, d, status, changes, resid, prio):
    d['verification'] = {"status": status, "changes": changes, "residualConcerns": resid, "spotCheckPriority": prio}
    with open(os.path.join(W, 'verified', i + '.json'), 'w') as f:
        json.dump(d, f, indent=1, ensure_ascii=False)

# Q33
d = load('Q33'); p = d['paper']
d['populations'] = ["Mixed / Unspecified"]
d['evidenceSummary'] = "PRISMA systematic review of 10 prospective randomized controlled trials published 2004-2019, including 292 patients who had or were planned to have ACL reconstruction. Among four protein or amino acid trials (177 patients), two found significant benefits in isokinetic strength or rehabilitation sessions needed to reach benchmarks and two found greater thigh hypertrophy than placebo, while one biopsy analysis and the glucosamine trial showed no benefit; creatine (60 patients), vitamin C and E (49 patients in one cohort) and testosterone (6 men) showed no benefit on muscle outcomes."
p['findings'] = "Among four protein or amino acid trials (177 patients), two reported significant advantages over placebo in isokinetic strength or in the number of rehabilitation sessions needed to reach benchmarks, two reported greater thigh hypertrophy, and one (Vidriero et al.) reported improved IKDC scores and less analgesic use; Holm et al.'s muscle biopsies showed no difference and the glucosamine trial found no benefit. One creatine trial (60 patients) found no between-group differences. Vitamin C and E trials found no benefit on serum cytokines or strength, peak isometric force was greater with placebo at three months, and biopsies showed more inflammatory cell infiltration in the vitamin group. One testosterone trial in six men found greater total lean mass at six weeks only, with no difference in injured-leg strength or clinical scores at any time point."
save('Q33', d, "CORRECTED", [
 "populations: 'Injured Athletes' applied to ACL reconstruction patients whose athletic status is not stated -> 'Mixed / Unspecified' only (patients, 'patients who underwent anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction')",
 "evidenceSummary/findings: implied all four protein trials showed benefit -> two showed significant strength or benchmark benefit, two showed hypertrophy, glucosamine trial and one biopsy analysis showed none ('the authors found no benefits with Glucosamine supplementation')",
 "findings: testosterone 'no benefit in the injured leg at 24 weeks' -> no injured-leg or clinical-score difference at any time point ('no differences ... regarding extensor strength of the injured leg or clinical scores at any point')"
], "Testosterone trial concerns a prescription hormone; the record states no benefit and safety limits, which a reviewer may want to confirm.", "high")

# Q34
d = load('Q34')
save('Q34', d, "VERIFIED", [], "", "normal")

# Q35
d = load('Q35'); p = d['paper']
p['findings'] = "Within each sex, no differences in sweat rate or sweat sodium, potassium or chloride concentration or content were found between crampers and non-crampers; female potassium content showed P = .03, which did not meet the study's P < .01 threshold. In American football, sweat rate and sodium, potassium and chloride content predicted cramp history (AUC 0.65-0.72, P <= .005); the authors also report that a sweat rate per body surface area above 0.75 L per hour per m2 carried about six times the odds of being cramp-prone, although that variable's AUC (0.62, P = .02) did not reach significance. With American football removed, no sweat variable predicted cramp history, and males lost more sweat and electrolytes than females."
p['limitations'] = "Cramp history was self-reported, and the authors did not separate local from whole-body cramps. Field conditions could not control hydration status, fluid type or duration, and sweat patches collected primary sweat that may overstate concentrations. No athlete cramped during testing, about 71% of football data came from off-season conditioning, and the authors note possible type II errors; the sixfold odds figure for sweat rate per body surface area comes from a variable whose AUC was not significant (Table 5)."
save('Q35', d, "CORRECTED", [
 "findings: presented the SR/BSA > 0.75 L/hr/m2 sixfold odds as a significant predictor -> noted its AUC was not significant (Table 5: 'SR/BSA 0.62 [0.49, 0.73] .02'; significance set at p < .01)",
 "limitations: removed the unneeded statement that abstract and results agree; added the SR/BSA caveat"
], "", "high")

# Q36
d = load('Q36'); p = d['paper']
d['synthesisCaution'] = "Staff could read the review's examples of elite practice, such as a marathon race plan or a train-low regimen, as proven methods to copy, when the authors say it remains to be shown whether elite athletes succeed because of or in spite of their nutrition practices."
p['findings'] = "Carbohydrate is the main fuel for most sports, and daily carbohydrate intake typically varies from about 2 to 12 g per kg body mass across training cycles. Train-low sessions augment cellular responses, but translation to performance has been less clear: early studies failed to detect superior performance, while better integration of train-low and train-high sessions has been linked to superior performance in subelite populations. Competition guidance cites carbohydrate intakes of 30-60 g per hour for events up to 2-3 hours and 60-90 g per hour for ultra-endurance events. The review notes that few supplements have robust evidence, citing caffeine, creatine, bicarbonate, beta-alanine and nitrate, and that some interventions, such as beetroot juice, appear less effective in elite competitors."
p['practicalImplications'] = "Staff can match carbohydrate, protein and fluid plans to the demands of each session and event rather than applying one diet. Train-low sessions are best treated as a targeted tool within a periodized plan, because their translation to performance has been less clear than their effect on cellular responses."
p['athleteDev'] = "Performance Application: the review supports periodizing carbohydrate and protein around training sessions and planning event fueling, including gut training and mouth rinsing. It also notes that many supplements lack robust evidence and that the performance benefit of train-low strategies is less clear than their cellular effects."
save('Q36', d, "CORRECTED", [
 "findings: 'some elite-athlete studies found no advantage' for train-low -> early studies failed to detect superior performance; benefit reported in subelite populations ('Early investigations failed to detect superior performance outcomes'; 'In subelite populations at least, better integration ... superior performance')",
 "synthesisCaution: authors 'describe them as case histories that do not prove the nutrition caused the result' -> authors say it remains to be determined whether elite athletes succeed 'because, or in spite, of their nutrition practices'",
 "practicalImplications/athleteDev: 'performance benefit is not established/unclear' -> 'less clear' ('the translation to performance enhancement has been less clear')"
], "", "normal")

# Q37
d = load('Q37'); p = d['paper']
d['evidenceSummary'] = "Narrative review in ACS Omega of the analytical chemistry used to detect and quantify WADA-listed synthetic peptides in doping control, covering the peptides on the prohibited list, reference-standard synthesis, sample pretreatment, LC-MS and high-resolution MS methods, and validation. The authors describe no systematic search, and the validation examples they cite were run mainly on urine, plasma and serum from clinical trials, pharmacokinetic or spiked samples, with athlete samples used less often."
d['screeningLimitations'] = "This is a narrative review of laboratory methods with no described search, and it reports no athlete outcomes or performance or health effects. Most cited validation work used clinical-trial, pharmacokinetic or spiked samples rather than routine athlete samples, so it says little about how these peptides affect athletes."
p['findings'] = "Peptide hormones, growth factors, insulins and vasopressin analogues are listed in WADA sections S2, S4 and S5, and insulins and similar peptides are hard to detect because of short half-lives and similarity to endogenous molecules. LC or reverse-phase SPE purification can yield synthetic peptides above 95% purity, and the authors propose solid-phase peptide synthesis as a route to in-house reference standards. Reversed-phase LC coupled to high-resolution MS (TOF or Orbitrap) is described as the preferred platform, and cited validation studies report limits of detection from about 0.02 to 20 ng/mL depending on peptide and matrix. The authors note that no specific validation guide has been established for peptides and that, unlike other doping agents, peptides lack adequate reference materials."
p['limitations'] = "The review is narrative and does not state how studies were selected. Its validation examples draw mainly on spiked samples, clinical trials or pharmacokinetic studies; athlete samples were used less often (one cited study used 209 athlete serum samples for IGF-1). The article reports no clinical outcomes or effects on athletes."
save('Q37', d, "CORRECTED", [
 "evidenceSummary/screeningLimitations/limitations: 'a few samples from athletes' -> athlete samples used less often than clinical-trial or pharmacokinetic samples ('The use of samples from athletes has also been reported, although to a lesser extent'; 'Seo et al. reported the use of 209 serum samples collected from athletes')",
 "findings: LOD range 'about 0.05 to 20 ng/mL' -> about 0.02 to 20 ng/mL (Table: desmopressin and vasopressin 'LOD = 20 pg/mL')",
 "findings: 'few peptide reference materials are certified' -> peptides lack adequate reference materials ('there are many reference materials used in antidoping analysis. Unfortunately, this is not the case for peptide-type doping agents')"
], "Relevance is borderline: this is an analytical chemistry review of doping detection with no athlete health or performance outcomes. A reviewer may judge it out of scope under exclusion reason (c).", "high")

# Q38
d = load('Q38')
save('Q38', d, "VERIFIED", [], "", "high")

# Q39
d = load('Q39')
save('Q39', d, "VERIFIED", [], "The source text also mentions Moreira et al. (2019) when describing missing sample characteristics, although that judo study is not one of the five included studies; this is an inconsistency in the paper.", "normal")

# Q40
d = load('Q40')
d['identityCheck'] = "The filename THEDEV~1.PDF is an 8.3 truncation consistent with the text title 'The development of a HAMstring InjuRy (HAMIR) index ... protocol for an observational cohort study' (BMC Sports Science, Medicine and Rehabilitation 2022;14:128, DOI 10.1186/s13102-022-00520-3)."
save('Q40', d, "CORRECTED", [
 "identityCheck: 'cannot be matched' -> the truncated name THEDEV matches the opening words of the text title 'The development of a HAMstring InjuRy (HAMIR) index'"
], "", "normal")
print("ok")
